destination.title: Can the Police Scan Your Home From the Street?

short25: The Supreme Court still called it a search of the home.
On a freezing night in January 1992, a federal agent sat in a car on a public street in Florence, Oregon.
He pointed a thermal-imaging device at Danny Kyllo's home and read the heat leaking off the walls.
The garage roof and one wall glowed hot — to the agent, the sign of grow lamps.
That helped win a warrant, and inside were over a hundred marijuana plants.
But the device never saw through the wall.
It only read heat already drifting into open air.
On June 11, 2001, the Court split five to four.
Justice Scalia wrote that using a device not in general public use to learn what's inside a home is a search that needs a warrant.
The dissent called it just reading heat off the outside.
But the majority drew a line at the front door it called firm, and bright.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: And the reason the case still matters lies in the phrase Scalia chose: technology "not in general public use." In 1992, the fight was over a heat camera the size of a lunchbox.

"At the very core" of the Fourth Amendment, he wrote, "stands the right of a man to retreat into his own home and there be free from unreasonable governmental intrusion." The home is not just another place the police might search.
And the Fourth Amendment, the Court said, draws a firm line at its entrance — a line that must be "not only firm but also bright." Then came the rule that made the case famous.
"Not in general public use" is a moving line.
It is a winter night in 1992, a little after three in the morning.
We treat the home as the one place the government cannot reach without a warrant.
So on January 16, 1992, a little after three in the morning, an agent named William Elliott sat in a car across the street with a thermal imaging device — an Agema Thermovision 210 .
He never touched the home, never entered it, never even set foot on the property .
On June 11, 2001, the Supreme Court gave its answer, and it was close — five justices to four .
And a search of a home, without a warrant, is presumptively unreasonable .

So the Court fixed the line at the wall itself: what the inside of your home holds is presumptively yours, and pulling it out with a special device is a search — whether that device reads heat, or something no one has invented yet .
The agent, he said, never went through the wall.
Whatever you call the heat, the purpose and the result were the same: the government learned what was going on inside a house without a warrant.
The lesson was not "you can never do this." It was "get a warrant first." That difference is the whole point.
The Constitution rarely tells the police they can never learn something.

When your private words travel as sound through the open air, or as a signal down a wire — into a glass phone booth on a public sidewalk, where anyone can see you, but no one is supposed to be listening?

lines.text: Scalia's rule turns on one phrase. Technology not in general public use. In 1992 that meant a heat camera the size of a lunchbox.
source_lines: In 1992, the fight was over a heat camera the size of a lunchbox.

lines.text: But not in general public use is a moving line. A device that is exotic today can sit in everyone's pocket tomorrow.
source_lines: "Not in general public use" is a moving line. A device that is exotic today can sit in everyone's pocket tomorrow

lines.text: And the more ordinary a technology becomes, the weaker your claim that using it invades your privacy. The Court protected the home against the future.

The Court protected the home against the future, but it tied that protection to a standard the future keeps rewriting

lines.text: Scalia's worry looked forward, not back. If the rule depended on how good today's device happened to be, privacy would shrink steadily.
source_lines: Scalia's worry looked forward, not back.
then privacy in the home would shrink a little every time a better machine came along

lines.text: Every year the tools for sensing what happens inside a home get cheaper, smaller, sharper. Drones overhead, cameras, devices that read through walls.
source_lines: Every year, the tools for sensing what happens inside a home get cheaper, smaller, and sharper — drones overhead, better cameras, devices that read signals through walls

lines.text: Kyllo is the case courts keep returning to when they ask how far the government can push those tools before it needs a warrant.
source_lines: Kyllo is the case courts keep returning to when they ask how far the government can push those tools before it needs a warrant

lines.text: So the question is not whether your home is protected. It is how long the device that watches it stays unusual.

shorts.angle: Kyllo never banned thermal imaging and never freed Danny Kyllo; it sent the case back with a narrower instruction than people remember.
shorts.avoids: The existing Short ends on the bright line at the front door as though the scan were simply forbidden; this cut is the limited order the Court actually issued.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Once the thermal evidence was set aside, did the warrant against Kyllo still stand?
shorts.loop_join: L5 states the general shape, and L1 returns as the concrete example of it: a search, yes, but no ban on the device.

lines.text: The Supreme Court called a heat scan of a house a search. It did not ban the device that did it.
source_lines: So the Court fixed the line at the wall itself: what the inside of your home holds is presumptively yours, and pulling it out with a special device is a search

lines.text: It did not ban thermal imaging. It did not erase the evidence against Kyllo for good.
source_lines: It did not ban thermal imaging. It did not erase the evidence against Kyllo for good.

lines.text: It sent the case back down with a narrower instruction. This kind of scan is a search, so it needs a warrant.
source_lines: It sent the case back down with a narrower instruction: this kind of scan is a search, so it needs a warrant

lines.text: The lesson was not you can never do this. It was get a warrant first. That difference is the whole point.
source_lines: The lesson was not "you can never do this." It was "get a warrant first." That difference is the whole point.

lines.text: The warrant that opened Kyllo's home did not rest on the scan alone. An informant's tip and unusually high electric bills stood beside it.
source_lines: Along with a tip from an informant and unusually high electric bills, the thermal scan helped Elliott convince a judge to sign a search warrant

lines.text: Inside, agents found what they expected: an indoor growing operation with more than a hundred marijuana plants. Kyllo was charged with manufacturing marijuana.
source_lines: When agents finally went inside, they found what they expected: an indoor growing operation with more than a hundred marijuana plants
Kyllo was charged with manufacturing marijuana.

lines.text: He pleaded guilty but kept his appeal. The lower court had to decide whether the warrant stood without the thermal evidence.

the lower court now had to decide whether the warrant still stood up once you set the thermal evidence aside

lines.text: The Fourth Amendment mostly sets a procedure, not a prohibition. Which is why rulings like this one sound bigger than they are.
